There are about three hundred known species of octopus. Most live in shallow ocean water, but some species are found in the deep sea. The body of an octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through very small openings. Its arms are covered with rows of suckers that help it grip surfaces and hold prey. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood that contains copper instead of iron. It breathes through gills. When threatened, an octopus can release a dark cloud of ink to confuse predators while it escapes. It can also change the color and texture of its skin to blend in with rocks, sand, or coral. Octopuses are considered one of the most intelligent groups of invertebrates. Scientists have shown they can solve puzzles, open jars, and use tools such as coconut shells for shelter. Most octopuses have short lives. Many species live only one or two years before they die.
